Ad extremum deposita omni verecundia per Tremoillium varia postulata Papæ ab opponentibus exposita, & inter hæc Concilium nationale, a quo, ut appellatio ad Generale fieri posset, pro fundamento stabilire ausi sunt. Sicque terminata fuit Cavalerii negotiatio.

§. 4.
*Appellatio ad Concilium Generale.*

Vaticana jam parabantur fulmina: Noaillius ab ipso Cardinalium Collegio purpura indignus censebatur. Nihilominus datum tempus adhuc resipiscendi, ex spe, quam ostenderant Opponentes confecto quodam doctrinæ schemate, quod cum ab acceptantibus probatum non fuit, scriptum eis trium columnarum, Janseniano illi olim simile obtulerunt, in quarum media ipsæ propositiones Quesnelli, ex una parte sensus obvius, ex altera alius quispiam Catholicus, vel certe excusationis patiens

Ne tamen una cum hoc negotio spes omnis iterum intercideret, Cardinalis Rohanus Aurelianensem permovit, ut ad 20. Nov. 1716. conventum Episcoporum indiceret, in quo Acceptantes aliquam explicationem Bullæ proponerent. Id ægerrime tulit Pontifex, & omni modo hoc consilium impedire aggressus, duo Brevia misit, unum Duci, quid Noaillio pararet, significans, alterum Sorbonæ, cui facultates & omnia privilegia ad tempus suspendit: cumque Tremoillius Cardinalibus, qui alias literas cum amicissimis hortatibus ad Noaillium dederant, & Papæ ipsi persuadere vellet, ut quidpiam de danda vel admittenda quadam explicatione adderetur; hic tertium Breve adjecit ad Episcopos acceptantes, quo eos hortatus est, ne se ab Opponentibus decipi sinant, & neque ullam a se Bullæ explicationem expectarent, nec ipsimet darent, aut admitterent. Verum Aurelianensis Cardinalium literas Noaillio non exhibuit, qui interea Parlamento Duacensi, quod Theses quasdam Constitutioni faventes suppressisset…

In the end, all modesty being laid aside, the various demands of the opponents were exposed to the Pope through Trémoille, and among these a national Council, from which they dared to establish as a foundation that an appeal to a General Council could be made. Truly Clement, to put an end to these tricks and frauds, answered in a few words: two paths remained for ending the composition, spontaneous submission or Canonical force. And thus the negotiation of Cavalier was terminated.

§. 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The bolts of the Vatican were already being prepared: Noailles was judged unworthy of the purple by the College of Cardinals itself. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having finished a certain draft of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by the acceptors, they offered them a document of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which the propositions of Quesnell were read, on one side the obvious meaning, on the other some other Catholic [meaning], or at least one patient of excuse

patient of excuse. But neither could that please, and glosses were added by the acceptors, by which they showed that the obvious meaning of the propositions was rightly condemned, and that they could not have another, except through a violent distortion. Lest, however, all hope perish again together with this business, Cardinal Rohan persuaded the Orléanais to indicate a convention of Bishops for November 20, 1716, in which the Acceptors might propose some explanation of the Bull. The Pontiff took this very badly, and, having attempted in every way to impede this counsel, he sent two Briefs, one to the Duke, signaling what he was preparing for Noailles, the other to the Sorbonne, whose faculties and all privileges he suspended for a time: and when Trémoille wanted to persuade the Cardinals, who had already given other letters with most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added concerning the giving or admitting of some explanation; he added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, by which he exhorted them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to expect any explanation of the Bull from him, nor to give or a…

The Pontiff took this very badly, and attempting in every way to hinder this plan, he sent two Briefs, one to the Duke, signaling what he was preparing for Noailles, the other to the Sorbonne, whose faculties and all privileges he suspended for a time: and when Tremoille wished to persuade the Cardinals, who had otherwise given letters with most friendly exhortations to Noailles, and the Pope himself, that something should be added regarding the giving or admitting of some explanation; he added a third Brief to the accepting Bishops, by which he exhorted them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the Opponents, and neither to expect any explanation of the Bull from him, nor to give or admit one themselves.
